title: Matrices, entries, and triangular form
section: Matrices and Matrix Algebra ▷ Dimensions and Matrix Operations
terms: matrix; matrix dimensions; matrix entry; row; column; diagonal entry; main diagonal; square matrix; upper triangular matrix; lower triangular matrix; zero matrix; matrix addition; scalar multiple; diagonal matrix.

exposition.text:
An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns; a is its entry in row i, column j. A square matrix
ij
has m = n, and its main diagonal consists of a . Upper triangular means a = 0 for i > j, and
ii ij
lower triangular means a = 0 for i < j. A diagonal matrix has zero entries away from its main
ij
diagonal.
Matrices of the same size add entrywise, and scalar multiplication acts on every entry. The zero
matrix is the additive identity. Counting the independently selectable entries gives dimensions
of structured matrix spaces: an upper triangular n × n matrix has n(n + 1)/2 free entries, while a
diagonal one has n. Constraints on entries can reduce these counts.
A matrix is strictly upper triangular if its entries on and below the diagonal vanish. Every
square matrix has a unique decomposition into a strictly upper triangular matrix and a lower
triangular matrix, obtained by assigning each entry to its permitted part. Extra symmetries
must be combined with forced zeros before counting free entries.

question.text:
How many entries of a real 5 × 5 upper triangular matrix with all diagonal entries fixed equal to
1 may be chosen independently?
(A) 5 (B) 10 (C) 15 (D) 20 (E) 25

solution.text:
Only entries strictly above the diagonal remain free. Their number is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. The
fixed diagonal does not contribute free choices.

question.text:
Real matrices A, B, C, D all have size 2 × 3 and satisfy 2A + B = C and A − B = D. Which
expression equals A + 2B?
(A) C + D (B) C − D (C) 2C − D (D) (C + 2D)/3 (E) (2C − D)/3

For an arbitrary real n × n matrix M, how many decompositions M = U + L exist when U is
upper triangular with every diagonal entry zero and L is lower triangular?
(A) None unless M is diagonal
(B) Exactly one
(C) Exactly n
(D) Infinitely many for every M
(E) One if M is symmetric, and none otherwise

solution.text:
Above the diagonal, L is zero, so U must copy M. On and below the diagonal, U is zero, so
L must copy M. This constructs a decomposition and forces every entry, proving unique-
ness. Without the zero-diagonal restriction the diagonal could be split in many ways.

solution.text:
Reversing both indices sends a position above the diagonal to one below it. The latter is
zero by triangularity, so every off-diagonal entry is zero. On the diagonal the symmetry
pairs positions 1, 9; 2, 8; 3, 7; and 4, 6, leaving position 5 alone. There are five independent
diagonal values.
